senses.definition: (geography, geology) One of the main contiguous landmasses, separated by water or geological features, on the surface of a planet, sometimes including its continental shelves and the islands on them.

quotes.text:
But I should turn mine ears and hear
The moanings of the homeless sea,
⁠The sound of streams that swift or slow
⁠Draw down Æonian hills, and sow
The dust of continents to be; […]
quotes.reference: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], “Canto XXXV”, in In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, page 54:

senses.definition: (sociogeography) Each of the traditional main regions into which the Earth’s land surface is divided, including both an extent of mainland and various conventionally associated islands, etc; namely, Africa, Europe, Asia, Australasia/Oceania, North America, South America, and Antarctica.

(obsolete in general sense) A large contiguous landmass as opposed to its islands, peninsulas, and so forth; mainland. Also specifically, the Old World continent of Europe–Asia–Africa: see the Continent.

quotes.text: No man is an Iland, intire of it ſelfe; euery man is a peece of the Continent, a part of the maine; […]
quotes.reference: 1624, John Donne, “17. Meditation”, in Deuotions upon Emergent Occasions, and Seuerall Steps in My Sicknes: […], London: […] A[ugustine] M[atthews] for Thomas Iones, →OCLC, pages 415–416:

senses.definition: (figurative) A large connected expanse of something in general.
(obsolete) Any continuous tract or area of land; country, connected region.
(obsolete) Land (as opposed to the water), dry land.

quotes.text: The carkas with the streame was carried downe, / But th’head fell backeward on the continent.
quotes.reference: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book III, Canto V”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London: […] [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:

senses.definition: (obsolete) The body or mass of a celestial body such as the sun or moon.
(obsolete) Container, vessel, something that holds or contains something else.
(obsolete) The principal or essential points of something viewed collectively: sum, summary, substance.

quotes.text:
[…] Here's the scroll,
The continent and summary of my fortune.
quotes.reference: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London: […] Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:

senses.definition: Exercising self-restraint; controlled, temperate with respect to one’s bodily needs or passions, especially sex.

quotes.text: Have a continent forbearance till the speed of his rage goes slower.
quotes.reference: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London: […] Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:

quotes.text: Their strength was the strength of men geographically beyond temptation: the poverty of Arabia made them simple, continent, enduring.

quotes.text: A celibate himself, he was of the opinion that marriage was something of a concession to human frailty, to save from fornication those who could not be continent, so it was better to marry than to burn with lust.

senses.definition: Having voluntary control over one’s urination or defecation.
(obsolete) Not interrupted; connected; continuous, whether in time or space.
